The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 4(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the valuation of assets was not a capital asset and that the assessee could not be assessed to income tax under the Act. The respondent was a Head Constable in the Department of the Central Government. He was promoted as a Head Constable on the basis of a departmental enquiry. He was found guilty of misconduct and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years. He was also awarded a fine of Rs.2,000. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of the Tribunal was not justified. The High court also held that the order was not justified and the order of punishment was not justified, and that the order passed by the Tribunal was liable to be set aside. The HighCourt also held that there was no error in the order of penalty. The High Courts in the appeal have held that the Tribunal had not properly considered the evidence adduced by the respondent and had not properly applied its mind to the evidence adduced before it. The High COurt has also held that since the respondent had not been given any opportunity to defend himself, he was not entitled to any relief. The High Cou rt has also held in favour of the respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in setting aside the order of conviction and sentence. [775F] 1.2 The High Court has not properly considered all the evidence adduced in the case. [776G] 1.3 The High Court had not properly appreciated the evidence adduced on behalf of the respondent and has not properly applied the principles of natural justice. [778G] 1:4 The High Court erred in setting aside an order of dismissal passed by the Tribu nal. [777G] 1 :5 The High Court is not justified in setting aside a finding of fact recorded by the Trib Tribu n nal. The High Commis sioner is not justified. [780G] 1.(a) The High Court should not have interfered with the order of sentence passed by the authorities below. [779G] (b) The High Courts should not have re examined the evidence adduced at the trial. [782G] (c) The High court should have interfered with an order of punishment passed by the authority below. [771G] (d) The High CO Court should have interfered in an order of penalty passed by the disciplinary author ity. [785G] (e) The High Cou nal should have interfered on the ground of violation of principles of natural Justice. [786G] (f) The High Com missioner should have interfered only on the ground that the order is not justified on the ground, that the order has been passed by the competent authority. [787G] (g) The High Powered Tribunal should have interfered if the order is vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [790G] (h) The High Cour t has not properly appreciated that the order in question was passed by the subordinate authority. [772G] (i) The High cour t has failed to consider the evidence adduced against the respondent. [791G] (ii) The High ol l Tribunal has not properly examined the evidence on record and has not applied its mind. [792G] (iii) The High ties have not properly applied their mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The High Powera t has not applied the principles laid down by the High Court. [793G] (iv) The High power of the Tribunal to interfere with the order passed in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction is not justified because the High Court has failed to appreciate the evidence adduced.

The petitioners are employees of the respondent Corporation. They are engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling food grains. They are employed in the respondent Corporation as a clerk in the respondent corporation. They are paid wages for the work done by them. They are also paid wages for their work. They are entitled to the same. They are further paid wages for work done by the respondent Corporation from time to time. The petitioners are also paid the same wages for the same work. The petitioners have filed the present petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the respondent Corporation to pay the same to the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the petitioners are entitled to be paid the same pay as they are entitled to get the same pay scale as they are paid the same scale as they were paid the same scales as they are being paid by the respondent corporation from time to the time of their appointment. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in State of U.P. vs Ram Kishan, ; and State of U P. vs Ram Krishan, ; , and State of Uttar Pradesh vs Ram Kishan and others, ; , referred to. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for the issue and the writ of certiorari quashing the impugned order. The respondent State has filed the present peti tion under Article 32. The petitioners submitted that the petitioners cannot be paid the salary as they were employed in the Corporation and that they are entitled for the same pay. The petitioners therefore, prayed that the writ of Mandamus be issued to the respondent corporation to pay the salary as the petitioners are working in that Corporation. The respondent corporation has also filed an affidavit stating that they are working as clerks in the respondent department. The petitioners submit that the petitioners will be entitled to the salary as per the Rules. The respondent has also filed affidavit stating that there is no provision in the Rules for payment of salary as they have been working in the corporation. The petitioners contested the petition. The respondent contended that the pay scales as claimed by the petitioners are not being paid to them. The respondent Corpora tional Corporation has also relied on the decisions of this Court. The petitioners ' case is that the petitioners who are working in a corporation are entitled to pay the wages as per the rules. The petitioners claim that they are paid wages as per Rules is not tenable. The petitioners had also relied on a decision of this court in State of Haryana vs Ram Kishan; , , and the decision of the Supreme Court in State 's case is not applicable to the petitioners as they are not working in the said corporation. The respondent have also relied on an earlier decision of this Co operative Court in State vs Ram Kishan ; , and the decisions of the Supreme Courts in State of Punjab vs Ram Kishan 's case.

The State was not justified in refusing to grant a stage carriage permit under section 57D(1). [795C] 3. The State had no authority to grant a temporary permit under section 58C(1), and the State was justified in refusing the grant of a permit under that section. [796C] 4. The State could not grant a permit to the applicants for a period of five years. The State cannot grant a permit in respect of a temporary permit. [797F] 5. The State has no power to refuse a permit under sub section (1) of section 57C. [799B] 6. The State is not entitled to grant a permanent permit under sub s.(1) of Section 57C. The respondent was a dealer in the State of Madras. The respondent was a registered dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was ultra vires the State Legislature. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act was ultravires the State Legislature and the State Legislature had no power to make a law for the recovery of tax. The Act was not ultravires. The Act did not provide for the recovery by the State Government. The Act does not provide for any other mode of recovery. The Act is a self contained Act and the Act does not contemplate any mode of recovery of tax in respect of the tax. The Legislature has no power to legislate in respect of tax. [657 H] (ii) The Act is not a self contained code and is not a law for recovery of tax, but is a self enacted code. The Act has no application to the case of a dealer who has been assessed to tax under the Act. The Act cannot be said to be a self contained Code. The Act, therefore, cannot be said, to be a law for collection of tax. It is not a tax. The legislature has no power under the Act to make a tax. [757 H] The Act is one of the modes of recovery of the tax and the Act is a law for a recovery of tax and the tax is not a penalty. The Act can be said to have been passed by the State Legislature under the Act and the tax has to be paid by the State.

The appellant was a member of the Indian State and was dismissed from service on the ground that he was not a member of a State. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the order was illegal and inoperative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal passed by the trial court was illegal and invalid. The High court was right in holding that the order passed by the High Court was illegal and the order was not liable to be set aside. [619 F] (ii) The order passed by a High Court was not a decree of a civil court. The High Courts were right in holding the order of the High Court. [620 A] (iii) The order was not a judgment of a civil Court. The High courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the order had been passed by a civil court and not by a civil Court, and that the order did not amount to a decree of civil court. [621 A] (iv) The order did not indicate that the order could not be set aside on the ground of a decree of the civil court. It was not a decision of a civil nature. [622 B] (v) The order could not, therefore, be set aside merely on the ground, that it was passed by a subordinate court. [722 B] In the present case, the order was passed by the subordinate court and not on the ground. The order was passed in a civil court, and not on a proper construction of the order. [723 B] (vi) The order made by the High court was not a final order of the civil Court. [724 B] (vii) The order in question was not a mere order of dismissal. [725 B] (viii) The order, therefore, was not a order of dismissal and was not a nullity. [726 B] (ix) The order under appeal, was not an order of dismissal but a decree of dismissal. The order of the subordinate court was not an interlocutory order.

The appellant, a lessee of the land in dispute, was granted a lease of the land to the respondents. The respondents, who were the lessees of the land, applied for the grant of a lease of land to the appellant for the purpose of obtaining the lease. The appellant, however, refused to grant the lease. In the meantime, the respondents filed a suit for possession of the land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the lease. On appeal, the High Court held in favour of the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellant was not a lessee of land. The respondents had not been able to prove that the appellant had been in possession of the lands. The appellant had not proved that the appellant 's title to the land was adverse to the respondents and the suit was barred by limitation. The appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act. The suit was not barred by limitation as the appellant had not established that the appellant has been in possession. The respondents were not entitled to any benefit of section 6 of the Limitation act. The appellant could not prove that the respondents had been in actual possession of the property. The respondents could not prove the title of the appellant. The appellant did not prove that he had been in continuous possession of the said land. The appellant 's case was that the respondents were in actual possession and enjoyment of the land and that the appellant did not know the title of them. The respondents did not prove the adverse possession. The appellant failed to prove that he was in actual possession. The High court was right in holding that the appellant could not establish that the respondents have been in actual physical possession of the disputed land. The High Courts were right in holding the respondents to be in actual possession, and that the respondents could not be said to be in continuous possession.

The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground that he was not a workman within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1958. The appellant was dismissed on the ground of misconduct. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground, inter alia, that the order of termination was illegal and void as it was not made in accordance with the rules of natural justice. The High Court held that the order was not made by the employer in accordance with law and that the order did not amount to punishment. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The order of dismissal was not made under the rules of the natural justice and was not made within the meaning Of section 2(u) of the Act. The order of termination is not made in compliance with the rules. The order was made in accordance to the rules of industrial justice. The order is not made by a employer in accordance to law. The order made by the Tribunal is not a punishment. The order does not amount to an punishment. The employer is not bound to make an order of dismissal. The order cannot be made by a workman in accordance with rules of natural Justice. The order must be made by the management in accordance with rule of natural justice and not by a workman who has been dismissed from service. The order can be made by an employer in accordance only by a workman whose services have been terminated. [657 H] The order of discharge is not a penalty. The order may be made by way of punishment if it is made in accordance only with rules of industrial law. The employer has to be given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The order has to be made by means of a written statement and the oral evidence adduced by the employer before the Tribunal. The order could not be made by any workman in accordance only when the workman has been dismissed. [658 H] The appellant was not a workmen within the meaningof section 2(s) of the . The order of the Tribunal was not made on the ground mentioned in the order. The order did not contain any reasons for the order. [659 H] The Tribunal was not justified in holding that the order made by it was not a punishment and that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. [660 H] The High Court was right in holding that it was not open to the employer to make an oral statement before the Tribunal and that the Tribunal was justified in holding the order of discharge. [655 H] The employer was not bound to give any reasons for its order. The Tribunal was right in not making an oral statement. [656 H] The termination of the appellant was illegal and invalid as it was made in violation of the rules of domestic justice. [654 H] The dismissal of the appellant from service was illegal and inoperative as it was in contravention of the rules. [653 H] The Industrial Tribunal was right when it was made to dismiss the appellant from services. The order passed by the Tribunal was therefore not liable to be quashed. [652 H] The appeal must be dismissed.

The respondent would be entitled to the salary for the aforesaid period of two periods of two years on the same date.

Court has erred in reversing an order of conviction passed by the High Court. [777G] 4. The High Judge has erred in not interfering with the findings of the Sessions Court. The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service of the State of Madras. He was a member in the Indian Administrative service of the State. He was appointed as a Judge of the High Court under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was also a member of a High Court under the Prevention of Anti Corruption Act, 1988. [703B C] 1.2 The High Court has not taken the view that there was no evidence to show that the appellant 's appointment was made by the Chief Justice of the High Courts. The High Courts have not taken the same view. The High court has not taken any view. [704C] 1.3 The High Court is not in error. The High Commis sioner of the High court has taken the view of the High Commisioner of that High Court. [705C] 1:4 The High Court had taken the view in the matter of taking cognizance of the offence under section 5 (1) (a) of the . The High Court, therefore, was in error. [706F] 1:5 The High Court in taking cognizance of an offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, has taken cognizance of the offences under section 5 of the Prevention and Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1984. The High 'Court has taken the same decision in the matter. [707F] 1.4 The High Courts are not in error on the face of the record. [708F] 1.(a) The High Court could take cognizance of the case under section 5 read with section 5(2) of the. Prevention of Corruption. [709F] (b) The High Courts in taking cognizance under section 5, read with section 161 of Indian Penal Code and taking cognizance of a case under section 161, read with Section 5(1)(d) of that Act. [710F] (c) The High court was in error on its face. [711F] (d) The High 's view that the High court was not in a position to take cognizance of an offences under section 161 read with section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act. [609F] 1(a) The question whether the High Court is in error in directing the appellant to take cognizance under section 161 is a question of fact. [712F] (e) The High Com missioner of the State is not a public officer within the meaning Of section 5(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code. [713F] (f) The High Powered Authority of the State has no power to take cognizance on the ground that the appellant is a public servant and that the power to take the cognizance of the crime is not in the nature of a public servant as defined in section 2(3) (d). [712G] (g) The High power of the State to take cognizance is not a judicial power. [715F] (h) The High.

The appellant was elected to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the West Bengal Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that the appellant was not a member of the Scheduled Castes and that he was not a candidate for election to the West West Bengal Legislative Council. The High Court held that the appellant had not been a member of Scheduled Castes and the appellant was entitled to be declared elected. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not an elector for the purpose of election to the Bihar Legislative Assembly. The High court was right in holding that the appellant 's name was not included in the list of Scheduled Castes. The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. The appellant had not challenged the election on the ground of his caste. The appellant 's caste was not included within the expression "Scheduled Castes" in the Schedule to the Constitution. The appellant could not be declared a member of any Scheduled Caste. [657 H] (ii) The appellant had been declared a member by the West Bengal Legislature. The appellant did not challenge the election on any ground. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to be elected. [658 H] (iii) The appellant ' caste was not a Scheduled Caste because the appellant was a candidate for the purpose for which the appellant was declared a member. The appellant therefore, was entitled to the election. [659 H] (iv) The appellant could be declared a candidate for a seat in the West Bengal State Legislative Assembly. [660 H] (v) The appellant did, in the appeal before the High Court, contend that the appellant could not have been declared a candidate. The High Courts were right in holding the appellant ' caste as a member of an Scheduled Caste. It was not open to the appellant to challenge the election. The appellant cannot be declared a person of the Scheduled Caste. There was no question of the appellant having been declared a person as a member. [655 H] (vi) The appellant, however, did not challenge his election on the grounds that he was a member. He did not challenge that election on the other hand was not a scheduled caste. The High 'Court was right in saying that the appellant did not include a person of a Scheduled caste. [656 H] (vii) The appellant having been a member in the Scheduled Caste, he could not be held to be a member of that Scheduled Caste. He did, therefore, challenge the election of a member on the ground, namely, that he was an elector for election to a West Bengal Legislative Legislative Assembly. He did also challenge the election in the High Court.

The appellant was a tenant of a flat in Bombay. The appellant was a sub tenant of the flat. The appellant had a right to occupy the flat. He was in possession of the flat and the appellant was in possession. The appellant 's case was that the appellant was a licensee of the flat in Bombay and that the appellant had no right to occupy it. The trial Magistrate convicted the appellant under section 3(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant 's right to occupy a flat was not extinguished by the provisions of section 3(2) of the Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The appellant was not a licensee of a flat. The right to occupy is a right to the use of the flat for the purpose of the business of the appellant. The right of the appellant to occupy the premises for the purpose for which he was a sub lessee is a right of the landlord to occupy the same. The right is a right which is a right in the landlord to enjoy the premises for a purpose other than for which he is a sub lessee. The right conferred by the section is a right not merely a right of a landlord but also a right to enjoy the same. [628 F G] The appellant was in occupation of the flat on the date of the agreement. The appellant could not be said to have committed the offence of committing the offence of cheating. The appellant did not commit the offence of forgery. The appellant committed the offence under section 3 (1)(a). The offence of cheating was committed by the appellant on the date when the agreement was executed. The appellant, therefore, committed the offence.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1976. The company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company had a number of employees of the company. The company claimed that the company was entitled to the benefit of the award of the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal held that the company had a right to the benefit under the award. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of Industrial Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award of industrial Tribunal was erroneous and that the award was bad in law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of Industrial Tribunals is not a mere piece of evidence and is not a piece of evidence. The award is not a rule of law. The award cannot be challenged on the ground that the award is bad in law because it is based on a wrong assumption. The award does not contain any provision for the award of a Tribunal. The award has to be read as a whole and it is not a case of error apparent on the face of the award. [799B] 2. The award in question is a piece of paper and is not based on any evidence. The Tribunal has to consider the evidence on record and come to the conclusion that the award has been made on a wrong basis. The Tribunal is not bound to consider the entire evidence on record. [701C] 3. The award was made on a correct assumption. The Tribunal had not considered the evidence on the record and come the conclusion that it was a case of erroneous assumption. The appellant has not been able to show that the award had been made on the wrong assumption. [702C] 4. The Tribunal was right in holding that the award made on a proper assumption was not a piece piece of evidence, and that the Tribunal was right, in holding that it was not a case where the award was made by the Tribunal.

The appellant, a private limited company, was a private limited Company, and was a private company. The appellant was a private Company. The respondents, who were workmen of the appellant, claimed that the appellant was entitled to the wages for the period of the contract, and that the appellant had not been paid the wages for that period. The appellant contended that the appellant 's claim was not maintainable. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a private company within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, because the appellant was not a private limited workman. The appellant had not made any claim for wages for the said period. The respondents were not entitled to any wages for the aforesaid period. The award of the Industrial Tribunal was not vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of the award. The award was not vitiated because the appellant had made any claim to wages for the same period. The order of the Industrial Court was not vitiated on the ground that the appellant did not make any claim for the same. The award did not suffer from any error of fact apparent on the record. The award therefore was not vitiated. The award could not be sustained because the appellant did make any claim to the wages of the respondents. The award, therefore, was not vitiated in law. The award is therefore, set aside. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, further, that the award was not a valid award and the appellant was a public limited company within the definition of section 2 (s) of that Act. The award does not suffer from the vice of any error of procedure apparent on the award. It is not open to the appellant to raise the question of law as to the validity of the award on the ground of want of jurisdiction. The award cannot be sustained because it is not a valid one. The award must be set aside on the ground, that the dispute is not a private dispute within the meaning Of section 2(k) of the Act. The appellant cannot raise the question as to the legality of the award, because the award is not a public dispute within the definition Of section 2 (k) of that section. The award can be set aside only on the ground mentioned in section 2(j) of the . The award is not vitiated because it is a public dispute. The award has to be set aside in the light of the principles laid down in the decisions of this Court in the case of M/s. M. P. Mills Ltd. vs The Workmen, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 8, followed.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 409, 467, 468 and 471 I.P.C. and section 409 I.P., and section 409, I.P, and section 409 read with section 34 I.P . The prosecution alleged that the appellant was a public servant and was not a public servant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged, inter alia, that the appellant had been in charge of the office of the Chief Engineer, and that he had been in the office of a Chief Engineer. The prosecution further alleged that the Chief Engineer had been in a position to discharge his duties as Chief Engineer and that he was not a servant of the Government. The prosecution also alleged that the sanction of the Government was not obtained by the appellant and that the sanction was obtained by the Chief Engineer. Held, that the sanction obtained by the Government was a sanction obtained by a public servant. The sanction was not obtained in the present case. The sanction obtained by an officer of the Government could not be obtained in the absence of sanction. The sanction could not be said to be a sanction obtained in the presence of the appellant. The sanction must be obtained in a manner which would be prejudicial to the public interest. The sanction is not a sanction obtained under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The sanction of the State Government was not a sanction. The fact that sanction was obtained in the course of the investigation of a case under section 409, 467 and 471 I .P.C., does not make the sanction a sanction.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in the State of Travancore Cochin. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee to tax on the profits of the business in the year 1949 50. The assessee claimed that the profits of a business carried on by it were not taxable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The High Court held that the profits were taxable under the Act. The High court held that the income of a business in the taxable territories was taxable under the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and that the profits in the taxable territory were taxable under section 2(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and that the income was taxable under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income of a firm carrying in the State was taxable under that section. The income of the business carried on in the State in the taxable State was taxable in the taxable state. The income was taxable in that State. The income in the taxable States was taxable under sub section (1) of section 2(2) of the Income tax Act. The income which was taxable under this sub section was taxable under it. The income could not be taxed under the Act because the income was not taxable under that sub section. [408 D] (ii) The income was not assessable under the Act as it was not taxable in the hands of the assessee. The income did not fall under the second part of section 2 (1) (b) of the income. The income, therefore, fell under the second sub section. The Income 'tax Officer was right in holding that the income did not come within the second part. [409 G H] (iii) The income in question was taxable under a second part of the income of an assessee. The High Courts were right in holding the income of that assessee. The question whether the income was assessable under the second proviso to section 2(3) of the Incometax Act was not one of fact. The High 'Court was right in saying that the income in question fell under the third proviso to section 3(3) (a).

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The respondent company was carrying on the manufacturing process of manufacturing sugar in the year 1959. The company had a factory at Bombay. The company applied for the retirement of its employees on the ground that the age of retirement was not less than 60 years. The company contended that the age was not less. The company raised a preliminary objection that the age fixed by the company was not less and that the age should be fixed at 60 years. Held, that the age for the purpose of gratuity was not less but less than 60. The age of retirement of the employees was not less, but less than 50 years. The age fixed by it was not less at 60 years and the age of superannuation was not less; the age of the employees could not be fixed at 58 years. The Tribunal was right in holding that the age prescribed by the company for the purpose was not less less than 60 but less than 55 years. The award of the Tribunal was not justified. The Tribunal had no power to award the age of 60 years. It was not correct to say that the age in the present case was less than 60 and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to award the retirement age of the workmen. The Tribunal has no power to impose the age of 58 years. It is not correct to contend that the age has been fixed at 60 and that it was not possible to hold that the age had been fixed at 58. The Tribunal is right in holding the age of 55 years.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The company was a public limited company and was a public company. The company had its registered office in the State of Punjab. The company, in its capacity as a public limited Company, was a public Company. The company 's name was included in the register of directors of the company. The Company was a public incorporated company. The Board of Directors of the company was a body corporate. The company did not carry on the business of the company and its directors were also directors of the Company. The Board was of the opinion that the company was not a public company within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act. The Board, however, did not carry out the functions of the Board. The Board also did not carry any of the functions of a public limited companies. The Board therefore, issued a notice to the company to show cause why the company should not be wound up. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Board and the Board. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board was not competent to issue a notice to show cause against the proposed action of the Board, and that the Board had no power to issue a show cause notice to the Company. Held, that the Board could not issue a showcause notice to the appellant. The Board could not be said to have acted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the company, and that it was not competent for the Board to issue a fresh show cause notice. The Board had no authority to issue a new show cause notice in the matter. The Board did not act in a manner which was prejudicial to the interest of the company in the interests of its shareholders. The Board 's order was not challenged in the High court. The Board must be held to be bad in law. The Board cannot be said to be bad for want of jurisdiction. The Board is not competent to pass a fresh showcause notice. The power to issue show cause notice is not a power to issue the show cause notice and the Board is not bound to issue a further show cause notice, and the Board cannot be held to have acted arbitrarily in issuing the show cause notices. The Board can issue a show show cause notice only in respect of the proposed action. The Board may issue a show Cause notice to the appellants. The Board has no authority to pass a new showcause notice in respect of proposed action.

The appellants were charged with offences under sections 302 and 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellants were in possession of the stolen property and were in possession thereof. The appellants were charged under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Evidence Act. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had committed the murder of the deceased and that the appellants and the others were in possession and that they were in possession. The prosecution relied on the evidence of the witnesses who were the eye witnesses to the occurrence. The High Court accepted the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 and convicted the appellants under section 302 and 201. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : The evidence of P,Ws. 1, 2 and 3 is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellants. The evidence of the eye witnesses is not sufficient in the case to prove the charge. The evidence is not sufficient for the purpose of proving the guilt of all the accused. The evidence in the case is not sufficient. The evidence must be sufficient to prove that the appellants committed the murder. The evidence should be sufficient to establish the guilt of each of the appellants and that the circumstances in which the crime was committed are such that the appellants could not be convicted. [657 H] The evidence of these witnesses is sufficient to prove their guilt. The evidence on record is sufficient to establish that the appellants did commit the murder. [658 H] The High Court was right in holding that the evidence of these two witnesses was sufficient to prove guilt of the accused.

The respondents claimed that the property in dispute was a private property and that the property was not a private property. The trial court held that the property had been acquired by the Raja and that the properties were not a private properties. The High Court held that the properties had been acquired for the purpose of the Raja and the properties were the property of the Raja, and that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of article 31(1) of the Constitution. The High court held that in the absence of any evidence to show that the property belonged to the Raja, the property was a private properties and that the respondents were not entitled under article 31(2) of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The property in dispute belonged to the appellants and the properties belonged to the respondents. The property in question was a private one and the properties in question were not the property of a private person. The property belonged to a private person and the properties had not been acquired for any other purpose. The property was not the property in question. The property had been taken over by the Raja. Therefore, the property in suit was not a public property. [608 D] (ii) The property was a public property and the properties could not be acquired for the purposes of the Raja 's estate. The property could not be said to belong to the appellants. The property did not belong to the respondents, and the properties did not belong in the appellants ' family. The property, therefore, belonged to the appellant. [609 G H] (iii) The property belonged not to the appellants but to the respondents and the properties which were acquired for the benefit of their family. The properties were not the properties of the Raja as the property was the property of an individual. The property which belonged to the respondent was not the properties in dispute. The property therefore, belonged not to him.

The respondent firm, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the business of manufacturing and selling food grains. The firm was carrying on the business of selling food grains and other food grains. On the basis of the partnership deed, the firm was dissolved and the firm was reconstituted. The firm, however, continued to carry on the business. The firm continued to carry out the business of supplying food grains and food grains. In the meanwhile, the firm, in its capacity as the sole proprietor of the firm, had been dissolved and the partnership deed was cancelled. The firm filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the District Magistrate, Jammu, contending that the firm had been dissolved by the dissolution of the firm and the partnership had been dissolved. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the firm was not dissolved by the constitution of the firm. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The firm had been reconstituted by the dissolution and the partnership was dissolved by the dissolved firm. The partnership deed was not a valid one and the partnership could not be dissolved by the expiry of the dissolution of partnership. [630B] 2. The firm could not be reconstituted by the expiry Of the dissolution of firm. The firm having been dissolved by a dissolution of the partnership, the firm could not have been dissolved by dissolution of the dissolved firm and the firm could be dissolved by a fresh dissolution of the Partnership. [631C] 3. The firm has been dissolved by virtue of the dissolution order of the partnership. The partnership was dissolved and it was dissolved by a resolution of the partnership dated December 12, 1979. The partnership had been reconstituted and the partnership continued to carry the business of the firm in its capacity. The partnership continued to be dissolved by dissolution. The partnership could not have dissolved by dissolution, and the partnership ceased to be dissolved. [632C] 4. The firm being dissolved by dissolution could not be revived by dissolution of partnership by the dissolution. [633F] 5. The firm is dissolved by dissolution and the firm is dissolved.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Bombay. The appellants were the successors in interest of the respondent. The respondent was the owner of certain properties. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Custodian. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of article 14 of the Constitution. The appellants appealed to this Court. Held, that the provisions of the Bombay Act were not applicable to the case. The provisions of the Act were not intended to be applied to the case because the provisions of section 14 were not intended for the protection of the interests of the appellants. The provisions were intended to be applicable to the cases of the appellants and the Custodian was competent to issue a notification under section 4 of the Act. The provisions in the Act were intended to apply to the case of the appellants, and the Custodian had no power to issue a notice under section 4. The appellants had no power under the Act to issue a fresh notification under section 6. The appellants could not be heard to say that the provisions in the Bombay Act applied to the cases where the appellants had no right to the property. The appellants did not, therefore, be heard to contend that the provisions were not intended in the Act. Held, further, that the appellants had not been heard to say anything more than what they had done. The provisions contained in the Bombay Ordinance were intended to have the effect of preventing the appellants from acting in any manner prejudicial to the interests of their security. The provisions did not apply to the cases in which the appellants had been granted a lease of the properties. The provisions, therefore, were intended to operate in the case of a person who was in possession of the property.

The expression any public limited Company" in section 3(h) is confined only for public limited company which is not confined either to private limited Companies or public sector corporations. [709F G] 8. The expression expression "private company", in section 2 (hh) is not confined not only to private limited limited companies but also to private limited corporations. [609F G; 709F G, 709F] 9. The expression the public limited Company is confined only when public sector undertakings have been confined to private sector undertakings. [710F G] 9. [709G H] 10. The expression a private limited Company is not confined exclusively to private limited undertakings and public sector undertaking which are not included in the definition of public limited companies, but also includes private limited companies or public sector companies. [712F G] 11.

The respondent was a Ruler of Rajasthan. He was granted a permit to the respondent for the import of certain goods. The respondent was granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due to him from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to the refund of the amount paid by him to the State of Rajasthan. The High court held that the State of Ajmer was entitled to refund of the amounts paid by him. The High, Court held that there was no liability to pay the amount due under the contract between the State of Jodhpur and the State of Jaipur. The High Courts also held that the amount paid was not a tax on the sale of goods and that the State was entitled to claim refund of the money paid by the State of Bikaner. The High 'Court also held that there could be no liability to refund the amount paid to the State. The High. Court also held that in the absence of any liability to refund, the State of Saurashtra was entitled to recover the amount paid under the contract. The HighCourt also held in favour of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The State of Ajmer could not be said to be a State within the meaning of article 31(2) of the Constitu tion. The State of Rajasthan could not be held to be a Ruler of the State. It was not necessary to decide whether the amount paid could be said to have been paid by the respondent to the State, because, the State was not entitled to claim the refund of that amount. The State was not a State within its meaning. The State could not be treated as a State within article 31(1) of the Consti tution. The State had no right to claim refund. The State did not claim the refund. The High was right in holding that the State had no liability to make the payment of the amount. The Highness was not right in holding the State ofRajasthan to be a successor in interest of the State, and that the amount was not a revenue receipt. [657 H] The State of Jodhpur vs The State of Jaipur, ; , followed. The State 's liability to refund was not a liability to pay tax on the sales of goods and the State was liable to pay tax. The State, therefore, was not entitled in the present case to claim refund on the sale price of goods. [658 H] The High Court was right in saying that the State could not claim refund on its sale price of the goods. The State cannot claim refund on that ground. [659 H] The question whether the State was a State within a meaning of article 12 of the Constitution was not one of fact. The High Power of the State to claim refund was not one which was not a matter of law. The State in the present appeal was not a party to the suit. It was only a State within it. The State contended that the State did not have the right to claim the amount paid. The High Burt was right in not allowing the appeal. The State urged that the State 's claim was not one for refund of the tax paid by the appellant. The High Curt was right. The State appealed to this Court. The question whether it was a State ' within the meaning Of article 12 of its Constitution was not raised before the High Court. The High Commis sioner of the State was right in contending that the State became a State within that meaning of article 13 of the Constitution and that the High Court was wrong in holding that it was not a law within the meaningof article 31(3) of the constitution.

The appellants, who were dealers in agricultural produce, challenged the validity of the Madras Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1953, on the ground that the Act was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the Act contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Act violated article 19(2) of the Constitu tion and that the impugned Act violated article 14 of the Constitution and that the provisions of the Act violated articles 19(1) (g) and 19(1). The appellants contended that the Act infringed articles 19(2)(g) and (g) of article 19 of the Constitution as it infringed articles 19 and 19(2). Held, that the Act did not contravene article 19(3) of the constitution and that the object of the Act was to provide for the regulation of the business of the traders and the regulation of their business and the regulation and control of the business was not in accordance with the provisions of articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution, and that the regulation and regulation of the trade and commerce in the State was not in conformity with the provisions Of the Act. The Act was not a law within the meaning of article 19 and was therefore ultra vires the Constitution. Held, further, that the impugned provisions contravened articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Act was not in conflict with the provisions contained in articles 19 and 30 of the Constitution; and the Act was therefore ultravires the Constitution. It was not open to the appellants to contend that the Act had contravened articles 19(3)(g) or 19(1), and that the rules contravened articles 19, 19(1 )(g) as it infringed the fundamental right guaranteed under article 19(6) of the Consti tution. The Act did not infringe the fundamental right of the appellants under article 19 (1)(g). The Act was therefore not ultra vires the provisions of section 19(1); and the Act violated the fundamental right under article 19. The Act violated articles 14 and 19(6). The Act did, therefore, contravene article 19 (6) of its Constitution. The Act contravened articles 19 (1) (f) and (vi) of the Con stitution and was therefore void. The Act infringed articles 14 and 31 of its Constitution and was therefore, ultra vires the Act.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and the High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence was not reliable. HELD : (i) The evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellants. The evidence of eye witnesses was sufficient to prove that the appellants were guilty of the offence of murder. The evidence was not sufficient for the Court to take the view that the evidence did not establish the guilt of appellants. The High court was wrong in taking the view that it was not necessary to take the contrary view. The High Courts were wrong in taking a contrary view. [657 H] (ii) The evidence was sufficient to establish the guilt. The High 'Court was wrong in relying on the evidence of a witness. The High. Court was wrong. The evidence in this case was not sufficient. The High judge was wrong in coming to the conclusion that the evidence in this particular case was not reliable, and the High court was right in taking the contrary view in the matter. [658 H] (iii) The evidence in the present case was not enough to prove the charge of murder. [659 H] (iv) The evidence did not show that the appellants had been guilty of the murder. [655 H] (vi) The evidence showed that the appellants knew the appellants and that they were likely to commit the murder.

The appellants were allotted land in the Punjab Government under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The appellants were allotted the land in dispute. In the present case the Custodian had not applied his mind to the facts of the case. The Custodian has not applied his minds to the facts and circumstances of the case and the Custodian had rightly rejected the application of the appellants under section 5 and the Custodian was competent under section 5, and the appellants could not be allowed to cancel the orders of cancellation.

The appellants were appointed as teachers in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Public service Commission, however recommended the names for appointment to posts of teachers. In the meanwhile, the Public Service Commis sioner, Uttar Pradesh, made a recommendation to the Public Service commission for the appointment of the appellants. The Public Public Service Commission recommended the names to the Public Services Commission. The High Court, however, directed the Public Service Commissions to consider the names of candidates for appointment. The Public services Commission, however did not accept it. The Public Employment Commission, however directed the Public Services Commissions to consider their names for appointment. In the meantime, the Public Services Commis sions were made. The Public Serv ice Commission, however rejected the recommendation of Public Service Commission and the Public ServiceCommission. The Public Interest Commission, however in the meanwhile, recommended the case of the candidates. The Public Sector Undertakings, however, did not accept their recommendation. The Public interest Commission, however by its order dated 27.3.1986, directed the State Government to consider the cases of the candidates in accordance with the rules. The High, however, held that the Public Service Tribunal had no jurisdiction to consider the question of the Public Interest Commission. Hence the appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. The Public Works Commission had no jurisdiction in the matter. The Public Engineering Commission had no power to consider the matter. [775F] 2. The appellant, who was the Mahant of the respondent, was the Mahant. He was the Mahant in the respondent 's estate. He died in the year 1970. The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due to him from the respondent. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the rule of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the appellant was the Mahant and was not entitled for the benefit of rule of the code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The rule of the High Courts is that the rule of law is not applicable to a case where the rule of abatement is not applicable. The rule of abatement applies to a case when the rule of succession is not applicable in a case where there is a vacancy in the office of the Mahant. The rule is applicable only where there is vacancy in the place of the Mahant and the vacancy is not filled in by the Mahant. [615 F G] In the instant case, the appellant was a Mahant and was entitled to the benefits of rule of abatement. The rule applies only where there are a vacancy in a place where there is an vacancy in the post of Mahant. [715 F G]. The rule of law applies only where the vacancy is filled in by a Mahant and not where there is no vacancy in the vacancy.

The appellant, a member of the Andhra Pradesh State Legislative Assembly, was compulsorily retired from service on the ground that he had not completed five years of service as on 31st March, 1979, and that he had attained the age of superannuation on 31st December, 1979. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated 30th March, 1979 under article 309 of the Constitution of India, which provided that the age of retirement of a member of a State Legislative Assembly shall be determined by the Government on the recommendations of the Commission. The Government issued a notification on 30th March 1979 under article 311(2) of the Constitution. The Government further issued a notification under article 309 on 30th April, 1979 under Article 309 of the Constitu tion. The Government also issued a notification in the nature of a notification dated 29th March, 1980 under article 309. The Government in its order dated 30th April 1980 had issued a notification for the purpose of fixing the age of compulsory retirement of the members of the State Legislative Assembly. The Government had issued a circular dated 30th May, 1980 under Article 309, which provided for the age of retirees of members of the Union Legislative Assembly. In the meantime, the Government issued a circular on 30th May 1980 under Article 162 of the Constitution, which provided the age of compulsorily retired from the service of the members. The Government, however, issued a notification to the effect that the age for compulsory retirement of members of State Legislative Assembly would be determined by Government on the recommendation of the Commission, and that the age would be determined on the recommendation by the Government. The Government however, issued another notification dated 30.4.1980 under Article 309. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground, inter alia, that the Government had no power to fix the age of retired members of the Central Legislative Assembly, and that it had no power under Article 309 to fix the date of retirement of members on the recommendation. The High Court held that the Government was not competent to fix the minimum age of retirement for members of the Legislative Assembly, that the age was determined by the Governor on the recommendation made by the Governor, and that, therefore, the Government had not acted in accordance with the provisions of Article 309. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Government was not justified in fixing the age for members of State Legislature, and that in the absence of any provision in the Act, the Government could not fix the age for the members of State Assembly. [615H; 716A] 2. The Government could not have fixed the age of the members on the recommendations made by the Commission. It was not open to the Government to fix the maximum age of retirement to the members of a State Legislature. [616B] 3. The Government has not given any reasons for fixing the age. The Government cannot fix the age on the recommendation, and that there was no justification for fixing the maximum age for members. [617B] 4. The Government is not justified in prescribing the age of 58 years for members of a Union Legislative Assembly, because, the Government has not fixed the age for a member of State Legislative Council. [618B] 5. The Government can fix the age at which the members of Parliament are to be retired. The Government may fix the age to be 58 years for the members. [718C] 6. The Government should fix the age in respect of members of a Legislative Assembly.

The appellants were dealers in oil seeds and oil seeds. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the sale of oil seeds and oils. The appellants challenged the validity of the sales tax authorities 's order. The High Court held that the sales tax was not a tax on the sales of oil seeds. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales were not a tax within the meaning of article 286(1) of the Constitution and that the sales of the oil seeds were not sales within the meaning Of article 286(2) of the Constitu tion. HELD: The sales tax authority was not competent to impose sales tax on sale of oil oil seeds and the sales were therefore not liable to tax. The sales of oil oil seed and oil seeds were therefore not taxable. The sales were therefore liable to tax under the Act. The sales must be held to be sales within the definition of the term "sale" in article 286(3) of the Consti tution. The sales in question were therefore not sales within article 286(4) of the Con tution. [601 B C] The sales of the goods were not sales outside the definition of "sale" under article 286(5) of the Indian Constitution. The sales could not be held to have been made by the sales of a oil seeds and that the sale was not a sale within the meaningof article 286(i) of the constitution. The sales made by the appellants were not sales of oil seed and oils within the meaning and the sales made by them were not sales in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The sales effected by them were therefore not exempt from tax under the provisions of the Act.

The appellant, a Hindu, was married to the respondent, who was a minor. The respondent filed a suit for maintenance against the appellant and the respondent. The High Court held that the respondent had not been able to prove that the respondent 's wife had been living separately and that the respondent could not be made liable to pay maintenance under section 127 of the Code. The High court held that the appellant had not been made liable to make the payment of maintenance under section 126 of the Code and that the appellant was not entitled for maintenance under section 128 of the Code, and that the order of the trial court was not sustainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant 's wife was not entitled under section 127(1) of the Code to make the payments of maintenance under the Code. The appellant 's husband was not entitled by section 127(2) of the code. The respondent had not made the payment of the maintenance under section 124 of the Code because he had not made any payment of maintenance to him. [776G] 3. The appellant had not made out a case for maintenance under the Hindu Law. The respondent was not a party to the proceedings before the trial court. The appellant was not a parties to the proceedings. The appellant could not be said to be a party to a proceeding. [777G] 4. The appellant has not made out any case for maintenance. The respondent has not made any case for the maintenance under the Act. [778G] 5. The appellant is not entitled to any maintenance under section 488 of the Code even though he has made the payment. [787G] 6. The appellant cannot be made liable for the maintenance of the wife under section 127. [790G] 7. The appellant, therefore, cannot be made to suffer from the vice of the respondent '. The appellant is a manufacturer of cotton fabrics. The appellant manufactured cotton fabrics from the appellant and sold the same to the appellant. The appellant claimed that the goods were not liable to excise duty under the Act. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Collector. The Tribunal held that the goods in question were liable to excise under the Act and that the goods could not be subjected to excise duty. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant was not liable to pay excise duty under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. On appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the goods had been subjected to excise duties. The Tribunal also held that the value of the goods was not liable for excise duty. On the question whether the goods were liable to duty under the provisions of the Act, the Tribunal referred the matter to the High Court. The words "cost" are used in the definition of " cost actually taken for determining whether the cost of such packing is taken into consideration for determining the valuation of the goods. The words used in the said section are not intended to be used in the inclusive definition of "value" and " cost actually paid" in sub clause (a) thereof. The petitioner company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The company was a public limited company and was carrying on business in the company. The company had been carrying on business of manufacturing and selling houses and other buildings. The company, however, was not in possession of the premises. The company filed a complaint against the company for the recovery of possession of the said houses. The company resisted the complaint on the ground that the company had not been in possession of any premises and that the company was not in occupation of any premises. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the company that the company could not be said to be in possession of a premises and that it was not in the possession of any other premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The company is not a public limited Company and is not a company within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. The company has been carrying on any business in the Company. The company cannot be said to have been in possession or in possession of that premises. The Company is not a private limited company within the definition of the expression 'public company '. The company being a company within section 2(2)(d) the company cannot be held to be in occupation of the premises and the company cannot claim any protection under section 12(1)(e) of the . [601B] 2. The company 's business is not a commercial activity. The company must be held to have been carrying on the business of manufacturing or selling houses and all buildings, whether in the nature of a business or not, are not in the occupation of the company. [601C] 3. The company could not have been in occupation of a premises for a long time. The company may be in occupation or in possession or under the control of the company, but it cannot be said that the company has been in occupation or under the management of the company and the company has not been in occupation thereof. [602C] 4. The company can be said to belong to the company and its employees. The company does not belong to the Company. It is not a 'public company" within the meaning Of section 2(3)(d) and the company is not in occupation or possession of any property. [603F] 5. The company in its capacity as a public limited corporation has been in possession and occupation of the property. The company therefore cannot be said in occupation of that property. [703F] 6. The company would be in possession and possession of the property and it cannot be held that the company is in possession of it. [604F] 7. The company should be in possession or possession of the company for a long period. The company will be in possession for a long long period.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, on the ground that the provisions of the Bombay Revenue Revenue Code, 1908, were not applicable to the case. The petitioner challenged the validity of the detention order on the ground, inter alia, that the provisions Of the Bombay Revenue Code, 1959, were not ultra vires the Constitution and that the provisions contravened article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned provisions were ultra vires the provisions of article 14 of Constitution and were not ultravi the Constitution. The provisions of the Act were not ultra ves the Constitution. It was not open to the petitioner to challenge the validity of a detention order on grounds which were not in accordance with the provisions of section 3(2) of the Act. The provisions Of the Act were ultra vires article 14 of its Constitution. The impugned provisions were not ultraves the Constitution and were therefore ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature.
